reason: Heads and capitula are described as cylindric.
The examples are mostly 'rounded' or 'rounded-discoid', which is not obtuse. The part is mixed (apex and disk).
Seeds and achenes can be cubic.
Mericarp sides can be pitted (foveate).
Isodiametric describes the surface or testa cells, not the seed. The bearer is wrong. A rule should assign it to the cell.
'In 2 series' counts the rows of the corona's parts, not the corona itself. A counted-parts rule is needed.
'hairs few' and 'stems few' count other things (hairs, stems), not parts of the stem. The bearer is wrong.
A tube or mouth can be constricted.
'margin ciliate' describes the margin of an organ, not a trichome. A trichome is not itself ciliated.
Corona lobes or segments can be filiform or threadlike.
Flat is a valid quality for apex and glands.
Ovule orientation can be horizontal.
Tepals can be narrow.
Lobes can be shallow.
The counts are of heads on branches or the rachis, not of the inflorescence. A counted-parts rule should handle this.
Calyx lobes can be persistent.
Indusia can be glabrous or hairy.
Papery texture is valid for this part.
Leaf sheaths can be soft.
This is the shape attribute, and the epichile has a shape.
The apex or portion can be trifid or tripartite.
Awns can be stiff or rigid.
An inflorescence axis can be pubescent.
PATO_0000001 is the root 'characteristic' term and too generic. The examples are mixed (straight, dichotomous, plane).
Indusia can be orbicular.
A petal can be lanceolate-triangular. Better handled by a rule that splits a compound shape.
The margin can be undulate.
Veinlets can be ascending.
A stem base can be flexuose or sinuous.
'Crown ovoid' is fine, but 'cime ovoïde' is a cyme. Ovoid (3-D) is also not ovate. A rule needs to tell the bearer apart and map ovoid separately.
A lip or lobe can be pendulous or drooping.
An acute or acuminate apex is a valid sharpness.
Parallelodromous is a venation pattern of the whole lamina. 'Lateral veins parallel' describes the relation between veins, so the bearer is wrong.
A perispore surface can be smooth.
A perispore can be hyaline (transparent).
Internodes have a length.
Achenes can be wrinkled.
Veinlets can be slender.
A pedicel or peduncle can be quadrangular.
Utricles can be obovate.
Nuts can be hairy.
Lobes and tips can be spatulate.
Parts can be dentate. Some examples ('apex with 2 teeth') are really counts of teeth.
The examples describe the perispore, lobes or laesurae, not the spore. The bearer is wrong.
The corolla tube can have window-like openings (fenestrate).
The statements say where limbidia are found, so the bearer is the limbidium and not this part.
The presence or absence of pistillate flowers is a standard pattern. Some 'nombreuses' examples are abundance.
Calyx lobes can be orbicular.
Cymbiform means boat-shaped, which is scaphoid, and perianth lobes can be that shape.
The examples are about irregular areoles, a venation pattern, not the spacing of vascular bundles. The part is wrong.
Capsules can be tomentose.
Lodicules can be present or absent.
Capitula can be oblong.
An apex or style branch can be obtuse.
A tube can be bent.
'Pinnate' describes the venation of the whole lamina. A rule would need to move it to the leaf lamina or to branching of the lateral veins.
A base can be decurrent.
Nectaries can be cup-shaped.
A palate or rim can be raised.
Lodicules can be linear.
